passages.t: Publicly available geology data are compiled to provide a common information base for resource development and regulatory decisions in the Cooper Basin region (Figure 1). This data guide gives examples of how the compiled data can be used. It supports a data package that presents core photographs, existing knowledge of the stratigraphy, and structural elements for the Cooper Basin and the overlying Simpson, Eromanga and Lake Eyre basins.

Stratigraphic frameworks capture the geological groups and formations that make up the sedimentary sequence in the Cooper Basin region. The Cooper Basin includes 2 stratigraphic groups. From deepest to shallowest, these are the Gidgealpa Group and the Nappamerri Group. The overlying Cuddapan Formation is considered part of the Simpson Basin instead of the Cooper Basin. Overlying the Cooper Basin are the geological formations of the Eromanga and Lake Eyre basins.

The frameworks include the stratigraphic intervals used by the Trusted Environmental and Geological Information (TEGI) Program. From the base of the Cooper Basin to the top of the Lake Eyre Basin, the sedimentary sequence is categorised into 16 play intervals for resource assessment mapping and 9 hydrostratigraphic intervals for characterising groundwater systems (Wainman et al., 2023).

Structural elements maps summarise where the sedimentary sequence has been deposited and later deformed by crustal movements. Structure information is used in assessing the geological potential for resources and interpreting groundwater flow and connectivity at the basin scale. The stratigraphic frameworks and structural elements provide the basic geological context for the Cooper Basin region geological, resource and environmental assessments.
Keywords: Cooper Basin, structure, seismic, boreholes, stratigraphy, core.

Figure 1. Geographic location of the Cooper Basin (purple) in central Queensland and the subsurface position of the Cooper Basin displayed conceptually. Note: The conceptual section displays basins along line A−A’ from 0 km to ~4.5 km subsurface.

The Cooper Basin occupies a total area of approximately 127,000 km². The basin is exposed at the surface in the east and north-east. In all other areas the basin lies beneath the Eromanga and Lake Eyre basins.

The subsurface geology of the Cooper Basin and its overlying basins is understood from 147,801 line km of 2D seismic data, 29,896 km² of 3D seismic data and 4,879 boreholes within the geological extent of the basin (Figure 2). 53% of boreholes exceed depths of 2,000 m. Borehole and seismic data help to define basin architecture. The Cooper Basin has a maximum modelled thickness of ~2,600 m. Up to ~3,000 m of sedimentary rocks of the Eromanga and Lake Eyre basins overlie the Cooper Basin.
Table 1 summarises key structural and geological information from the Cooper Basin region, including geological age, tectonic setting and structures.

Figure 2 data: Derived from All borehole and well locations – Queensland (Queensland Government, 2022a); Seismic survey 2D – Queensland – Queensland (Queensland Government, 2022b); 3D seismic data – Queensland (Queensland Government, 2022c) and South Australian Resources Information Gateway (SARIG) (2022). The Cooper Basin extents are from the Australian Geological Provinces Database (Raymond et al., 2018). Background image is the GEODATA 9 second digital elevation model, version 3 (hillshade) (Hutchinson et al., 2008).

Structural elements: Crustal movements shape geological basins during and after sediment deposition. Structural elements are the basic geological features produced by crustal deformation, such as basement, faults and folds (i.e. synclines and anticlines). Structural elements maps capture the key geological features created by deformation events. Structural offsets affect regional groundwater flow and are key to locating areas of resource potential. The geologic basement is the surface beneath which sedimentary rocks are not found.

Stratigraphic frameworks: The arrangement and description of rock layers (strata) in an area are captured in a stratigraphic framework. Strata may be organised into units based primarily on rock character (lithostratigraphy), geological age (biostratigraphy and chronostratigraphy), or rocks of the same geological age bound by surfaces of erosion and deposition (sequence stratigraphy). The frameworks included in this package display lithostratigraphic and, where available, other stratigraphic arrangements for the Cooper and overlying basins.

Core photography: Rock may be collected during borehole drilling as a cylindrical core sample. Core is used to measure rock properties, such as lithology, grain size and porosity. These properties are important for evaluating groundwater systems and hydrocarbon resource potential. Core is also used to support stratigraphic and gross depositional environment interpretations. Core images are provided in this data package as a cross-reference to the interpretations that underlie the groundwater and resource assessments of key intervals.
Several structural elements are mapped in the subsurface Cooper Basin region (Figure 3).

The locations of maximum sediment thickness, or depocentres, in the Cooper Basin include the Patchawarra and Nappamerri troughs in South Australia and the Windorah Trough and Ullenbury Depression in Queensland.

Key structures (folds, faults or basement structures underneath the basin) controlling basin architecture include the Warra Ridge, Packsaddle Ridge and the Durham Downs Anticline. The Murteree Ridge, for example, is a basement high in the Cooper Basin and influenced structure in the Eromanga and Lake Eyre basins.

Some of the structural elements shown in Figure 3 are expressed in the overlying Eromanga Basin. Structural elements may influence aquifer connectivity and are relevant for the groundwater conceptual model of the Cooper Basin region (Hostetler et al., 2023). They also influence areas where conventional hydrocarbon resources maybe trapped.

Figure 3 data: The structural elements are combined for the Cooper, Eromanga and Lake Eyre basins. Depth to basement is taken from Hall et al. (2015). Faults are from 3DGEO (2014) and Great Artesian Basin major geological structural elements (2013). The names of structural elements are from Owens et al. (2020).
Figure 3. Cooper Basin region structural elements imposed on a surface map showing depth to the base of the Cooper Basin. Note: Depth is m AHD.

Stratigraphic charts are included in this data package for each of the sedimentary basins indicated in Figure 4 for the Cooper Basin region. The charts display groups and formations and their dominant lithology, plotted against geological time. These are arranged into play intervals and hydrostratigraphic intervals to the level that current knowledge allows. Play intervals and hydrostratigraphic intervals are used by the Trusted Environmental and Geological Information (TEGI) Program for resource and groundwater assessments. Where relevant, other related stratigraphic information is included, along with information on potential petroleum, geological storage of carbon, and groundwater systems.

Play intervals are defined as a set of rocks formed by the same geologic circumstances, bounded by major geological events. These events may be prolonged periods of non- deposition or erosion (hiatuses) or tectonic events. For this reason, the charts include depositional environments, basin phases and tectonic events with time.
Hydrostratigraphic intervals are grouped geological units that have a similar character influencing the distribution and movement of groundwater, including aquifers.

Petroleum systems describe the geological elements necessary to generate and store hydrocarbons. Source rock, reservoir and seal intervals are relevant for conventional hydrocarbon exploration. Strata that are targets for unconventional hydrocarbon exploration are also indicated.
Geological storage of carbon (GSC) describes the geological elements required for the injection and containment of carbon dioxide underground. Intervals with GSC potential are shown.

Figure 4. Simplified stratigraphic chart of sedimentary basins in the Cooper Basin region and underlying pre-Permian rocks. The Big Lake Suite are granites present under the basin. Note: Red lines denote hiatuses.

Representative images of core samples are used to illustrate the dominant rock types and other geological features of stratigraphic intervals. Observations are used to make interpretations of gross depositional environments and help to guide resource and groundwater assessments.

Figure 5 is an example from the Patchawarra Play interval (1,869– 1,871 metres below ground level from the Le Chiffre 1 core and 2,620–2,622 m from the Talaq 1 core), including time-equivalent rocks known as Granite Wash (3,042.21– 3,044.02 m from the Moomba 236 core). These cores host sandstone, siltstone, claystone and coal lithologies and are interpreted to represent fluviolacustrine and mire environments. Granite wash rocks represent weathered granite deposited in alluvial fans.

Figure 5 data: Core photography of Le Chiffre 1, Talaq 1 and Moomba 236, taken from PEPS SA (2022). Cores stored at the Drillcore Reference Library, Adelaide, South Australia. See appendices for core photographs from other play intervals.
Figure 5. Example core image from the Cooper Basin Patchawarra Play interval.

Geological data within this package is mostly based on publicly available borehole data. Confidence in these data is calculated and mapped using the following parameters: the date each borehole was acquired; the total depth the borehole was drilled to; and the spatial separation between boreholes. Data confidence in the Cooper Basin region subsurface geology presented in this package is low to medium. Borehole confidence is high on the Wooloo Trough and on the Murteree Ridge in the South Australian sector of the basin, as many are deep and are closely spaced. Borehole confidence is lower in the Queensland sector of the basin due to low borehole density.
The low density of borehole data in Queensland limits meaningful interpretations of basin architecture and sedimentary geometries in this sector of the Cooper Basin region.

To address data and knowledge gaps, complementary activities could include well log conditioning; refinement of stratigraphic frameworks using new robust age data; and drilling of a stratigraphic borehole in the Queensland sector of the basin to improve understanding of the Cooper Basin regional geology.
Figure 6. Geological data confidence map for the Cooper Basin region, based on the drill date, total depth, and spatial density of boreholes.
Figure 6 data: Derived from All borehole and well locations – Queensland (Queensland Government, 2022a) and the South Australian Resources Information Gateway (SARIG) (2022).

Geoscience Australia and CSIRO have tried to make the information in this product as accurate as possible. However, it does not guarantee that the information is totally accurate or complete. Therefore, you should not solely rely on this information when making a commercial decision.
Data compilation date: October 2022.
2D Seismic: Linear method for imaging the subsurface using controlled seismic energy sources and receivers at the surface.

Activity: For the purposes of spatial causal networks, an activity is a planned event associated with development of a driver. For example, some activities associated with the green hydrogen driver are civil construction, electrochemical hydrogen production and decommissioning and rehabilitation.

Adavale Basin: The Adavale Basin geological province is a lower Devonian to lower Carboniferous geological sedimentary basin in southern central Queensland. Its maximum thickness is more than 5,500 m and it occurs at depths between 2,900 m and 7,500 m. It is entirely subsurface, overlain by the Galilee, Eromanga and Lake Eyre basins. It occupies a total area of approximately 60,000 km2.
Aeolian: Relating to sediment deposition or erosion by the wind.
Alluvial fan: A fan-shaped wedge of sediment that typically accumulates on land where a stream emerges from a steep canyon onto a flat area. In map view it has the shape of an open fan.

Alluvium: Loose, unconsolidated (not cemented together into a solid rock), soil or sediments (from sands to large boulders), eroded, deposited and reshaped by water in some form in a non- marine setting.
Anticline: A fold in rock strata with a convex upward shape. The rocks in the core of an anticline are the oldest.
Aquifer: Rock or sediment in a formation, group of formations, or part of a formation that is saturated and sufficiently permeable to transmit quantities of water to bores and springs.
Aquitard: A geological formation that may contain groundwater but is not capable of transmitting significant quantities of it under normal hydraulic gradients. May function as a confining bed.
Artesian: Within a confined aquifers where the water levels rises above the level of the aquifer. Can also be used to indicate where the water level in a bore rises above the ground level.
Assessment extent (AE): The geographic area defined for each assessment type to constrain the area of investigation.

Asset: An entity that has value to the community and, for the purposes of spatial causal networks, is associated with a region. An asset is a store of value and may be managed and/or used to maintain and/or produce further value. An asset may have many values associated with it that can be measured from a range of perspectives; for example, the values of a wetland can be measured from ecological, sociocultural and economic perspectives.

Avoidance: Averting the risk by deciding not to start or continue with the activity that gives rise to the risk. For the purposes of spatial causal networks, the decision not to start an activity is mandated by the locally relevant legislation

Back-arc basin: A zone of tectonic enlargement, and substantial, and strongly asymmetric, sedimentation. A back-arc basin forms when an island arc is split along the line of its magmatic axis, forming a remnant arc, which then glides away. Well-developed back-arc basins widen by back-arc spreading, which is thought to resemble normal oceanic crust formation, but in conjunction with a subducting plate.
Basalt: The most common volcanic rock on Earth. Composed of essential calcic plagioclase and pyroxene, sometimes with olivine, feldspathoids or interstitial quartz.
Baseflow index (BFI): The ratio of long-term mean portion of the streamflow, which contains groundwater flow and flow from other delayed sources, to the total streamflow.

Biostratigraphy: Biostratigraphy is the branch of stratigraphy that uses fossils to establish relative ages of rock and correlate successions of sedimentary rocks within and between depositional basins.
Borehole: A narrow, artificially constructed hole or cavity used to intercept a specified rock unit or resource at depth.
Bore screen: The construction component of a bore that allows groundwater to enter e.g. casing with slots or holes. Also known as the screen interval.

Bowen Basin: The Bowen Basin geological province is a lower Permian to Middle Triassic geological sedimentary basin in eastern Queensland. It is up to 10,000 m thick and occurs at depths between 0 and 10,000 m. It is overlain in the south by the Surat Basin and in the north by Cenozoic extensional basins. It occupies a total area of approximately 160,000 km2.

Carbon capture: The capture of CO from stationary emissions sources such as power stations, natural gas₂ production, fossil fuel hydrogen production and industrial facilities such as steel or cement manufacturing plants.

Carbon storage: The injection of CO underground into a suitable geological formation for permanent₂ storage, such as saline aquifers (e.g. sandstones that are filled with brine), depleted oil or gas fields, and potentially in other types of rocks such as deep coal seams or basalts.
Catchment: The land area draining to a point of interest, such as a water storage or monitoring site on a watercourse.

Causal pathway: For the purposes of spatial causal networks, the logical chain of events, either planned or unplanned, that link unconventional gas development and potential impacts on water and the environment.
Causal pathway group: Causal pathways with similar attributes (e.g. landscape management) that are grouped for further analysis.
Cenozoic: An interval of geological time from 66 million years ago to present. It is divided into the Paleogene Period (66–23 million years ago) and Neogene Period (23 million years ago to present).
Charge: In petroleum geoscience, a 'charge' refers to the volume of expelled petroleum available. for entrapment.
Chronostratigraphy: Refers to the correlation of rock units using absolute ages derived from geochronology.

Conceptual model: An abstraction or simplification of reality that describes the most important components and processes of natural and/or anthropogenic systems, and their response to interactions with extrinsic activities or stressors. They provide a transparent and general representation of how complex systems work, and identify gaps or differences in understanding. They are often used as the basis for further modelling, form an important backdrop for assessment and evaluation, and typically have a key role in communication. Conceptual models may take many forms, including descriptive, influence diagram and pictorial representations.

Confined aquifer: An aquifer that is confined between two aquifers. An aquifer below the land surface that is saturated with water. Layers of impermeable material are both above and below the aquifer, causing it to be under pressure so that when the aquifer is penetrated by a well, the water will rise above the top of the aquifer.
Consequence: The outcome of an event and has an effect on objectives.

Contaminant: A biological or chemical substance or entity that is not normally present in a system or any unusual concentration (high or low) of a naturally occurring substance that has the potential to produce an adverse effect in a biological system.
Contamination: An increase in the concentration of a biological, chemical or physical property that has the potential to produce an adverse effect in a biological system.
Contraction: Shrinkage of geological units from cooling or tectonic forces.

Cooper Basin: The Cooper Basin geological province is an upper Carboniferous to Middle Triassic geological sedimentary basin that is up to 2,500 m thick and occurs at depths between 850 m and 4,800 m. It is overlain completely by the Eromanga Basin and partly by the Lake Eyre Basin. Most of the Cooper Basin is in south-west Queensland and north-east South Australia, and includes a small area of New South Wales at Cameron Corner. It occupies a total area of approximately 130,000 km2, including 95,740 km2 in Queensland, 34,310 km2 in SA and 8 km2 in New South Wales.

Co-produced water: A term used in the oil and gas industry to describe water that is produced as a by-product along with the oil and gas. Oil and gas reservoirs often have water as well as hydrocarbons, sometimes in a zone that lies under the hydrocarbons, and sometimes in the same zone with the oil and gas. The terms 'co-produced water' and 'produced water' are sometimes used interchangeably by government and industry. However, in this assessment, 'co-produced water' refers to the large amounts of water produced as a by- product of coal seam gas development, whereas 'produced water' is used to describe water produced as a by-product along with the oil and gas.
Core photographs: High resolution images of rock cores taken by a camera.
Cumulative impact: For the purposes of spatial causal networks, total impact on endpoints from multiple stressors, and their interactions, due to multiple developments in multiple industries.
Current controls: The methods or actions currently planned, or in place, to detect hazards when they occur or to reduce the likelihood and/or consequences of these hazards should they occur.

Deltaic: Deposition of sediment in a delta. A delta is a low, nearly flat area near the mouth of a river, commonly forming a fan-shaped plain that can extend beyond the coast into deep water. Deltas form in lakes and oceans when sediment supplied by a stream or river overwhelms that removed by tides, waves, and currents.
Depocentre: An area or site of maximum deposition and associated with the thickest part of any specified stratigraphic unit in a depositional basin.
Depression: In geology, a syncline-like depression; associated with tectonic downwarping. A result of isostacy, subduction or similar.

Diamictite: A type of lithified sedimentary rock that consists of non-sorted to poorly sorted terrigenous sediment containing particles that range in size from clay to boulders, suspended in a matrix of mudstone or sandstone.
Diapir: A relatively mobile mass of rock (typically salt) that intrudes into pre-existing rocks.

Direct relationship: A direct or positive relationship along a causal pathway, where the starting node and the next node both increase or decrease together: an increase in node A increases node B or a decrease in node A decreases node B.
Drawdown: A lowering of the groundwater level (caused, for example, by pumping).

Drilling fluid: Circulating fluid that lifts rock cuttings from the wellbore to the surface during the drilling operation. Also functions to cool down the drill bit, and is a component of well control.
Driver: The major external driving forces that have large-scale influences on natural systems. Drivers can be natural or anthropogenic forces.
Ecological values: Values associated with estuarine, freshwater and marine aquatic ecosystems, groundwater-dependent and terrestrial ecosystems.

Economic values: Values associated with benefits derived from the production, consumption and accumulation of resources for activities, such as agriculture, aquaculture, drinking water supply, industry or intensive development and tourism.

Ecosystem: A dynamic complex of plant, animal, and micro-organism communities and their non-living environment interacting as a functional unit. Note: ecosystems include those that are human-influenced such as rural and urban ecosystems.

Effect: A specific type of an impact (any change resulting from prior events). For the purposes of the impact analysis for the spatial causal networks, an effect is the change in node 'B' due to a change in node 'A'; for example, a change in vegetation removal due to a change in civil construction.

Eromanga Basin: The Eromanga Basin geological province is an Early Jurassic to Late Cretaceous geological sedimentary basin that covers much of Queensland, north-eastern South Australia, southern NT and north-western NSW. It has a maximum encountered thickness of 2,500 m.

Extended region (ER): The geographic area defined for each environmental, surface water and groundwater assessment to constrain additional data discovery and to allow potential impacts immediately adjacent to the region to be considered.
Extension: A geological process formed by the stretching of a planetary body's crust or lithosphere.

Extraction: The removal of water for use from waterways or aquifers (including storages) by pumping or gravity channels. In the oil and gas industry, extraction refers to the removal of oil and gas from its reservoir rock.

Extrusive volcanism: Extrusive volcanism results from when magma exits and cools above (or very near) the Earth's surface to form igneous rocks. These are the rocks that form at erupting volcanoes and oozing fissures.
Fault: A fracture or zone of fractures in the Earth’s crust along which rocks on one side were displaced relative to those on the other side.

Flowback: The process of allowing fluids and entrained solids to flow from a well following a treatment, either in preparation for a subsequent phase of treatment or in preparation for clean up and returning the well to production. The flowback period begins when material introduced into the well during the treatment returns to the surface following hydraulic fracturing or refracturing. The flowback period ends when either the well is shut in and permanently disconnected from the flowback equipment, or at the start up of production.
Flowback water: The fluids and entrained solids that emerge from a well during flowback. Typically includes a mix of drilling, hydraulic fracturing and formation fluids.
Fluvial: Sediments or other geologic features formed by streams.

Fluvioglacial: Erosion or deposition caused by flowing meltwater, from melting glaciers, ice sheets and ice caps. Glacial meltwater is usually very rich in sediment, which increases its erosive power.
Fluviolacustrine: Sediments or other geologic features formed partly by streams and partly by lakes.
Fold: A curve or bend of a formerly planar structure, such as rock strata or bedding planes, that generally results from deformation.
Foreland: Low-lying region that is adjacent and parallel to a mountain belt and formed as the result of the collision of tectonic plates.
Formation: Rock layers that have common physical characteristics (lithology) deposited during a specific period of geological time.

Formation fluid: Any fluid within the pores of the rock. It may be water, oil, gas or a mixture. Formation water in shallow aquifers can be fresh. Formation water in deeper layers of rock is typically saline.

Galilee Basin: The Galilee Basin geological province is a middle Carboniferous to Middle Triassic geological sedimentary basin in central Queensland. It has a maximum encountered thickness of 2,800 m and occurs at depths between 0 and 2,800 m. It is overlain partly by the Eromanga, Lake Eyre and smaller Cenozoic basins. It occupies a total area of approximately 249,000 km2.
Geological interval: Geological time periods, including Eons, Era, Period and Epochs, experienced in the Earth's history.

Geological storage: CO is injected deep underground into a suitable geological formation for permanent₂ storage, such as saline aquifers (e.g. sandstones that are filled with brine), depleted oil or gas fields, and potentially in other types of rocks such as deep coal seams or basalts.
Glacial: Relating to the presence of ice, notably in the form of glaciers or ice sheets.

Glaciolacustrine sediment: Deposits and landforms composed of suspended material brought by meltwater streams flowing into lakes bordering the glacier, such as deltas, kame deltas, and varved sediments.
Gross depositional environments: A series of genetically related packages of sediments that formed under similar geological (physical, biological or chemical) conditions.

Groundwater: Water occurring naturally below ground level (whether stored in or flowing through aquifers or within low-permeability aquitards), or water occurring at a place below ground that has been pumped, diverted or released to that place for storage there. This does not include water held in underground tanks, pipes or other works.

Groundwater- dependent ecosystem: Natural ecosystems that require access to groundwater to meet all or some of their water requirements on a permanent or intermittent basis, so as to maintain their communities of plants and animals, ecosystem processes and ecosystem services.

Groundwater level: Measurements from the top of the ground surface to the groundwater level. Positive values are below the ground surface. Negative values are above the ground surface and indicate artesian conditions.

passages.h: Glossary: Groundwater- surface water connectivity/ interactions
passages.t: Groundwater- surface water connectivity/ interactions: The direction and magnitude of flow between water resources located above and below ground.
Groundwater system: A groundwater reservoir and its contained water. Also, the collective hydrodynamic and geochemical processes at work in the reservoir.
Hazard: A source of risk, for which likelihood, consequence and mitigation options need to be evaluated.

Hiatus: The cessation in deposition of sediments, resulting in an interval(s) during which no strata form, or an erosional surface(s) within the stratigraphic sequence representing a gap in the rock record.

Hydraulic fracturing fluid: The fluid injected into a well for hydraulic fracturing. Consists of a primary carrier fluid (usually water or a gel), a proppant such as sand, and chemicals to modify the fluid properties.
Hydraulic head: The height of a column of water above a reference datum such as mean sea level.
Hydrostratigraphic interval: Any soil or rock unit or zone which by virtue of its hydraulic properties has a distinct influence on the storage or movement of groundwater.

Impact: The difference between what could happen due to changes associated with development of a driver and what would happen without development of that driver. For the purposes of spatial causal networks, impacts are adverse changes to endpoints that represent the ecological, economic and/or social values to be protected. Impacts can be a direct or indirect consequence of single or multiple developments. For example, an impact of unconventional gas resource development could be a decrease in the persistence of the grey grasswren.
Intraformational seals: A seal rock that exists within a geological formation.
Intracratonic: Within a major structural geological unit of the Earth's crust, consisting of a large stable mass of rock.

Invasive: A species that (i) has successfully established outside its natural range as a result of human actions, deliberate or inadvertent, that have enabled it to overcome biogeographical barriers; (ii) gone on to has spread rapidly over substantial distances from sites of introduction; and (iii) has the potential to have harmful effects on components of the natural environment.

Inverse relationship: For the purposes of spatial causal networks, an inverse or negative relationship is where if one node increases, the next node decreases: an increase in node A causes a decrease in node B or a decrease in node A causes an increase in node B. In contrast, a direct or positive relationship is where both nodes increase or decrease together.

Isochore: A contour connecting points of equal true vertical thickness of strata, formations, reservoirs or other rock units. A map that displays isochores is an isochore map. The terms isopach and isopach map are incorrectly used interchangeably to describe isochores and isochore maps. Isopachs and isochores are equivalent only if the rock layer is horizontal.

Isopachs: A contour that connects points of equal thickness. Commonly, the isopachs, or contours that make up an isopach map, display the stratigraphic thickness of a rock unit as opposed to the true vertical thickness. Isopachs are true stratigraphic thicknesses; i.e., perpendicular to bedding surfaces.
Lacustrine: Sediments or other geologic features formed by lakes.

Lake Eyre Basin: The Lake Eyre Basin geological province contains Cenozoic terrestrial sedimentary rocks within the Lake Eyre surface water catchment. It covers parts of northern and eastern South Australia, south-eastern Northern Territory, western Queensland and north-western New South Wales. Where it overlies the Cooper Basin, it is less than 300 m thick.
Lateral facies: Two or more facies that are found to be adjacent within the rock record, with no unconformities, then they must have also been deposited laterally in formation.

Level of concern: A rating that describes assessment of potential impacts on an endpoint in the causal network. It represents the residual risk, as it is based on evaluation of likelihood and consequence and takes into account mitigation strategies, such as compliance with existing regulatory controls and operational practice.
Likelihood: Chance that something might happen.
Link: Cause-and-effect relationship between two nodes in a causal network.
Lithology: The description of rocks, especially in hand specimen and in outcrop, on the basis of characteristics such as colour, mineralogical composition and grain size.
Lithostratigraphy: The organisation of rock strata into units based on their lithology.
Management: For the purposes of spatial causal networks, a coordinated set of activities and methods used to minimise and control risks.

Material change: For the purposes of spatial causal networks, an expression of the severity or consequence of a change. A change that exceeds defined thresholds in terms of magnitude, extent, duration, timing or frequency that is likely to require local-scale assessment, mitigation and monitoring.
Metasediments: A rock of sedimentary origin that has been subjected to metamorphism.
Millidarcies: Measurement of permeability used to measure the ability of a rock to transmit fluids.
Mire: A tract or area of wet, swampy ground that contains deep accumulations of decomposed organic material, or peat.
Mitigation: Minimising the risk by removing the risk source, or changing the likelihood or consequences of the activity that gives rise to the risk.
Neutron log: A type of wireline log used in drill holes that measures hydrogen concentrations in a rock formation to estimate permeability and porosity.
Node: Component of a causal network, which can include a driver, activity, stressor, process, endpoint or asset.
north Bowen Basin: The north Bowen Basin region refers to any part of the Bowen Basin north of the Surat Basin margin.
Orogenic: Relating to deformation of the earth's crust during mountain building.
Outcrop: Total area over which a rock formation occurs at the Earth's surface, whether visibly exposed or not.

Permeability: The measure of the ability of a rock, soil or sediment to yield or transmit a fluid. The magnitude of permeability depends largely on the porosity and the interconnectivity of pores and spaces in the ground.
Petrophysical: The physical properties of rocks, in this context, as measured by well logs.
Play: An age or time-equivalent interval of sedimentary rock formed by the same geological processes used to identify areas of resource potential.
Polyphase: Consisting of or occurring in a number of separate tectonic stages.
Porosity: The proportion of the volume of rock consisting of pores, usually expressed as a percentage of the total rock or soil mass.
Potential distribution: The geographic range in which suitable habitat might be found for a species, modelled from presence-only occurrence records and environmental variables.
Potentiometric surface: An imaginary surface representing the static head of ground water in an aquifer; or, in the case of unconfined aquifers, the water table.
Process: For the purposes of spatial causal networks, a naturally occurring mechanism (e.g. floodplain inundation) that could change a characteristic of an endpoint.

Produced water: A term used in the oil and gas industry to describe water that is produced as a by product along with the oil and gas. Oil and gas reservoirs often have water as well as hydrocarbons, sometimes in a zone that lies under the hydrocarbons, and sometimes in the same zone with the oil and gas. The terms 'co-produced water' and 'produced water' are sometimes used interchangeably by government and industry. However, in this assessment, 'produced water' is used to describe water produced as a by product along with the oil and gas, whereas 'co-produced water' refers to the large amounts of water produced as a by-product of coal seam gas development.
Proglacial: In front of, at, or immediately beyond the margin of a glacier or ice sheet.
Prospectivity: The likelihood of making a petroleum discovery, and then also the likelihood that any discovery can be commercially developed.

Red beds: Red beds is a term referred to sediments or sedimentary rocks composed primarily of sandstone, siltstone, or shale that are predominantly red in colour due to the presence of iron oxides. These sedimentary rocks are deposited in hot arid climates under oxidizing conditions.

Reduced standing water level: A water level that describes the groundwater level elevation relative to the Australian Height Datum (AHD). This is the standard height datum used in Australia. It sets mean sea level as zero elevation. Positive values are above mean sea level and negative values are below.
Resource development: Activities required for economic production or consumption. For the purposes of the TEGI program, this includes energy, mineral and water resources.

Risk: The effect of uncertainty on objectives (AS/NZS ISO 31000:2009). This involves assessing the potential consequences and likelihood of impacts to environmental and human values that may stem from an action, under the uncertainty caused by variability and incomplete knowledge of the system of interest.
Seal rock: A relatively impermeable rock, commonly shale, anhydrite or salt, that forms a barrier or cap above and around reservoir rock such that fluids cannot migrate beyond the reservoir.
Sedimentary rock: A relatively impermeable rock, commonly shale, anhydrite or salt, that forms a barrier or cap above and around reservoir rock such that fluids cannot migrate beyond the reservoir.
Seismic: The principal geophysical method used to image the subsurface in both land and marine environments using sound signals.

Sequence stratigraphy: The study of rock relationships within a chronostratigraphic framework of repetitive genetically related strata bounded by surfaces of erosion or deposition or their correlative conformities.
Severity: Magnitude of an impact.
Sociocultural values: Values associated with aesthetic, cultural and spiritual beliefs, human health and recreation or amenity values.
Sonic log: A type of wireline log used in drill holes that emits sound waves which start at the source, travels through a formation, and return back to the receiver.

Strata: A generalised term used in reference to a group of rock layers. Strata when plural, stratum when singular. These layers can be distinguished from layers above them and below them by differences in mineral composition, grain size, colour, fossil content, grain orientation or other characteristic.
Stratigraphic framework: A series of erosional and depositional surfaces that enclose and subdivide the sedimentary bodies or sequences of the stratigraphic section.
Stressor: For the purposes of spatial causal networks, a stressor is a physical, chemical or biological agent, environmental condition or external stimulus that might contribute to an impact.
Structural complexity: An increased variance of planar feature orientations, such as bedding or faults, in response to deformation events.

Structural elements: Geological features produced by deformation of the Earth's crust, such as a fold or a fault. It also refers to features within a rock, including fractures or bedding surfaces, or more generally, the spatial arrangement of rocks.
Structural high: Topographic or bathymetric high caused by faulting and/or folding.
Structural offsets: A displacement between points on either side of a fault, which can range from millimetres to kilometres.

Structure: The general disposition, attitude, arrangement, or relative position of the rock masses of an area; the sum total of the structural features of an area, consequent upon such deformational processes as faulting, folding, and igneous intrusion.
Supercritical fluid: A fluid at a temperature and pressure above it's critical point that has the properties of both a gas and a liquid.
Surfaces: Lines of equal elevation or depth for a selected marker horizon.
Surface water: Surface-expressed waters that are either permanent or ephemeral.
Syncline: A trough-shaped fold with youngest strata in the centre.
Synclinorium: A large syncline on which minor folds are superimposed.
Tectonic: Related to the structure and deformation of the earth's crust and the forces that produce such deformation.
Terminoglacial: Accumulation of sediments that forms just in-front of an ice mass.
Thermal subsidence: Mechanism of subsidence in which conductive cooling of the mantle thickens the lithosphere and causes it to decrease in elevation.
Topography: The configuration of a surface including its relief and the position of its natural and man- made features.

Trap: A geologic feature that permits an accumulation of liquid or gas (e.g. natural gas, water, oil, injected CO ) and prevents its escape. Traps may be structural (e.g. domes,₂ anticlines), stratigraphic (pinchouts, permeability changes) or combinations of both.
True Stratigraphic Thickness (TST): The distance between the top and base of a unit measured perpendicular to the top.
True Vertical Thickness (TVT): The measured thickness in a vertical well (or along a vertical traverse) is the true vertical thickness.
Unconfined aquifer: An aquifer whose upper water surface (water table) is at atmospheric pressure, and thus is able to rise and fall.

Vitrinite reflectance: Is the proportion of incident light reflected from a polished vitrinite surface. Vitrinite is a maceral (an organic component) of coal. As vitrinite is heated in the earth during burial, it systematically changes its reflective properties.
Volcaniclastic: Geological material composed chiefly of fragments of volcanic origin, as agglomerate, tuff, and certain other rocks; pyroclastic.
Volcanics: Relating to or produced by a volcano or volcanoes.

Wastewater: Used water from any combination of domestic, industrial, commercial or agricultural activities, and any sewer inflow or sewer infiltration. It can contain physical, chemical and biological pollutants. For the purposes of the TEGI Program, it can include used drilling fluids, flowback water (drilling, hydraulic fracturing and formation fluids), produced water (shale and tight gas resource development), co-produced water (coal seam gas development), process water (processing of hydrocarbons), or brine from desalination (green hydrogen development).

Watercourse: A river, creek or other natural watercourse (whether modified or not) in which water is contained or flows (whether permanently or from time to time); and includes: (i) a dam or reservoir that collects water flowing in a watercourse; (ii) a lake or wetland through which water flows; (iii) a channel into which the water of a watercourse has been diverted; (iv) part of a watercourse; and (v) an estuary through which water flows.
Well completion report: A report summarising the activities related to the drilling and installation of wells.
Wireline log: Continuous measurements of geological formation properties with electrically powered instruments to infer properties and make decisions about drilling and production operations.

passages.t: Publicly available geology data are compiled to provide a common information base for resource development and regulatory decisions in the Adavale Basin region (Figure 1). This data guide gives examples of how the compiled data can be used. It supports a data package that presents core photographs, existing knowledge of the stratigraphy, and structural elements for the Adavale Basin and the overlying Galilee, Eromanga, Lake Eyre and other Cenozoic basins. Stratigraphic frameworks capture the geological groups and formations that make up the sedimentary sequence in the Adavale Basin region. The Adavale Basin includes 9 stratigraphic formations (Wainman et al., 2023). Overlying the Adavale Basin are the geological formations of the Galilee, Eromanga, Lake Eyre and other Cenozoic basins. The frameworks include the stratigraphic intervals used by the Trusted Environmental and Geological Information (TEGI) Program. From the base of the Adavale Basin to the top of overlying Cenozoic basins, the sedimentary sequence is categorised into 24 play intervals for resource assessment mapping and 12 hydrostratigraphic intervals for characterising groundwater systems (Wainman et al., 2023).

Structural elements maps summarise where the sedimentary sequence has been deposited and later deformed by crustal movements. Structure information is used in assessing the geological potential for resources and interpreting groundwater flow and connectivity at the basin scale. The stratigraphic frameworks and structural elements provide the basic geological context for the Adavale Basin region resource and environmental assessments. Keywords: Adavale Basin, structure, seismic, boreholes, stratigraphy, core.

Figure 1. Geographic location of the Adavale Basin (brown, cross-hatched) in central Queensland, and the subsurface position of the Adavale Basin displayed conceptually. Note: The conceptual section displays basins along line A−A’ from 0 km to ~4.5 km subsurface.

The Adavale Basin occupies a total area of approximately 60,000 km². The basin lies beneath the Galilee, Eromanga and Lake Eyre basins. The subsurface geology of the Adavale Basin and its overlying basins is understood from 16,993 line km of 2D seismic data. 45 boreholes sample the Adavale Basin. Borehole and seismic data help to define basin architecture. The Adavale Basin has an estimated maximum modelled thickness of ~4,800 m. Some other estimates suggest the Adavale Basin succession could be up to 8,500 m thick. Up to ~2,680 m of sedimentary rocks of Galilee, Eromanga and Lake Eyre basins overlie the Adavale Basin. Table 1 summarises key structural and geological information from the Adavale Basin region, including geological age, tectonic setting and structures.

Figure 2. Distribution of 2D seismic survey lines and borehole locations in the Adavale Basin region and surrounds. Figure 2 data: Derived from All borehole and well locations – Queensland (Queensland Government, 2022a); Seismic survey 2D – Queensland (Queensland Government, 2022b). The Adavale Basin extents are from the Australian Geological Provinces Database (Raymond et al., 2018). Background image is the GEODATA 9 second digital elevation model, version 3 (hillshade) (Hutchinson et al., 2008).

Table 1. Summary of key structural and geological information from the Adavale Basin region. Age: Early Devonian (Pragian) (~411 Ma) to Late Devonian (Famennian) (~365 Ma); Area: 60,000 km² of south-west Queensland; Maximum thickness: No consensus; >4,800 m (modelled); Maximum depth to base (m AHD): No consensus; ~7,000 m; Tectonic setting: No consensus. Back-arc (Early-Middle Devonian) and foreland (Middle Devonian to Late Devonian) phases. Considered intracratonic by others; Key structures: Canaway Fault, Pleasant Creek Arch, Canaway Fault, Warrego Fault; Basin overlies: Neoproterozoic – Early Palaeozoic metasediments of the Thomson Fold Belt and/or Ordovician volcanics and Silurian granites; Basin underlies: Galilee Basin, Eromanga Basin, Lake Eyre Basin; Basins adjacent: Darling Basin, Belyando Basin, Drummond Basin, Warrabin Trough.
Notes: m AHD = metres with respect to the Australian Height Datum.

Structural elements: Crustal movements shape geological basins during and after sediment deposition. Structural elements are the basic geological features produced by crustal deformation, such as basement, faults and folds (i.e. synclines and anticlines). Structural elements maps capture the key geological features created by deformation events. Structural offsets affect regional groundwater flow and are key to locating areas of resource potential. The geologic basement is the surface beneath which sedimentary rocks are not found. Stratigraphic frameworks: The arrangement and description of rock layers (strata) in an area are captured in a stratigraphic framework. Strata may be organised into units based primarily on rock character (lithostratigraphy), geological age (biostratigraphy and chronostratigraphy), or rocks of the same geological age bound by surfaces of erosion and deposition (sequence stratigraphy). The frameworks included in this package display lithostratigraphic and, where available, other stratigraphic arrangements for the Adavale and overlying basins.

Core photography: Rock may be collected during borehole drilling as a cylindrical core sample. Core is used to measure rock properties, such as lithology, grain size and porosity. These properties are important for evaluating groundwater systems and hydrocarbon resource potential. Core is also used to support stratigraphic and gross depositional environment interpretations. Core images are provided in this data package as a cross-reference to the interpretations that underlie the groundwater and resource assessments of key intervals.

Several structural elements are mapped in the subsurface Adavale Basin region, mainly in the west and south (Figure 3). Locations of maximum sediment thickness, or depocentres, in the Adavale Basin include the main depocentre in the centre of the basin, the Cooladdi Trough in the south and Westgate Trough in the eastern Adavale Basin. Key structures (folds, faults or basement structures) controlling basin architecture include the Pleasant Creek Arch, the Ravensbourne Arch and the Canaway Fault. The Canaway Fault coincides with the western margin of the Adavale Basin and separates it from the Warrabin Trough (not shown). The Pleasant Creek Arch is a basement high that influenced basin architecture in the Adavale Basin. Some of the structural elements shown in Figure 3 are expressed in the overlying Galilee and Eromanga basins. Structural elements may influence aquifer connectivity and are relevant for the groundwater conceptual model of the Adavale Basin region (Hostetler et al., 2023). They also influence areas where conventional hydrocarbon resources maybe trapped.

Figure 3. Adavale Basin region structural imposed on a surface map showing depth to the base of the Adavale Basin. Note: Depth is m AHD. Figure 3 data: Faults are taken and/or derived from Adavale Basin 3D Geological Modelling (Wang and Patterson, 2022). Depth to basement is derived from OZ SEEBASE® 2021, Geognostics (2021). Structural elements are taken from Troup and Talebi (2019) and McKillop (2013).

Stratigraphic charts are included in this data package for each of the sedimentary basins indicated in Figure 4 for the Adavale Basin region. The charts display groups and formations and their dominant lithology, plotted against geological time. These are arranged into play intervals and hydrostratigraphic intervals to the level that current knowledge allows. Play intervals and hydrostratigraphic intervals are used by the Trusted Environmental and Geological Information (TEGI) Program for resource and groundwater assessments. Where relevant, other related stratigraphic information is included, along with information on potential petroleum, geological storage of carbon, and groundwater systems. Play intervals are defined as a set of rocks formed by the same geologic circumstances, bounded by major geological events. These events may be prolonged periods of non-deposition or erosion (hiatuses) or tectonic events. For this reason, the charts include depositional environments, basin phases and tectonic events with time.

Hydrostratigraphic intervals are grouped geological units that have a similar character influencing the distribution and movement of groundwater, including aquifers. Petroleum systems describe the geological elements necessary to generate and store hydrocarbons. Source rock, reservoir and seal intervals are relevant for conventional hydrocarbon exploration. Strata that are targets for unconventional hydrocarbon exploration are also indicated. Geological storage of carbon (GSC) describes the geological elements required for the injection and containment of carbon dioxide underground. Intervals with GSC potential are shown.

Figure 5. Example core image from the Adavale Basin Log Creek Play interval. Figure 5 data: Core photography of Bury 1 and Gilmore 1 obtained by Carmine Wainman. Cores stored at the Australian National Core and Sample Collection, Canberra, ACT. See appendices for core photographs from other play intervals. We acknowledge the staff at the Geoscience Australia core libraries for their assistance with sampling.

Figure 4. Simplified stratigraphic chart of sedimentary basins in the Adavale Basin region and underlying pre-Devonian rocks. Note: Red lines denote hiatuses. Figure 4 data: Gradstein et al. (2020). See metadata statements and appendices for source information.

Representative images of core samples are used to illustrate the dominant rock types and other geological features of stratigraphic intervals. Observations are used to make interpretations of gross depositional environments and help to guide resource and groundwater assessments. Figure. 5 displays examples of core from the Log Creek Play interval (2,695.79–2,695.91 metres below ground level, and 2,696.05–2696.14 m in the Bury 1 core); and 3,778.70–3,778.80 m, and 4,018.61–4,018 m in the Gilmore 1 core). These cores host sandstone, claystone, diamictite and limestone lithologies and are interpreted to represent fluvial and shallow marine environments.

Geological data within this package is mostly based on open-source borehole data. Confidence in these data (Figure 6) is calculated and mapped using the following parameters, the total depth the borehole was drilled to, and the spatial separation between boreholes. Data confidence in the Adavale Basin region subsurface geology presented in this package remains low due to the low density of borehole data outside of the Gilmore Gas Field (area of high confidence, Figure 6) and the low number of boreholes that intersects rocks of the Adavale Basin. Twenty seven boreholes sample rocks equivalent to the Buckabie Formation or older. Low borehole density, with few reaching the base of the Adavale Basin, limits meaningful interpretations of sedimentary architectures and confident, regional interpretations of gross depositional environments. To address data and knowledge gaps, complementary activities could include well log conditioning and refinement of stratigraphic frameworks with new robust age data; and activities such as drilling a stratigraphic borehole that intersects the deeper play intervals (e.g. Gumbardo Play interval) to improve understanding of the Adavale Basin regional geology.

passages.t: Publicly available geology data are compiled to provide a common information base for resource development and regulatory decisions in the Galilee Basin region (Figure 1). This data guide gives examples of how the compiled data can be used. It supports a data package that presents core photographs, existing knowledge of the stratigraphy, and structural elements for the Galilee Basin and the overlying Eromanga, Lake Eyre and other Cenozoic basins. Stratigraphic frameworks capture the geological groups and formations that make up the sedimentary sequence in the Galilee Basin region. The Galilee Basin includes 4 stratigraphic groups. From deepest to shallowest, these are the Joe Joe Group, Betts Creek group, Rewan Group and Clematis Group. Overlying the Galilee Basin are the geological formations of the Eromanga, Lake Eyre and other Cenozoic basins. The frameworks include the stratigraphic intervals used by the Trusted Environmental and Geological Information (TEGI) Program. From the base of the Galilee Basin to the top of overlying Cenozoic basins, the sedimentary sequence is categorised into 15 play intervals for resource assessment mapping and 11 hydrostratigraphic intervals for characterising groundwater systems (Wainman et al., 2023). Structural elements maps summarise where the sedimentary sequence has been deposited and later deformed by crustal movements.

Structure information is used in assessing the geological potential for resources and interpreting groundwater flow and connectivity at the basin scale. The stratigraphic frameworks and structural elements provide the basic geological context for the Galilee Basin region geological, resource and environmental assessments. Keywords: Galilee Basin, structure, seismic, boreholes, stratigraphy, core.

Figure 1. Geographic location of the Galilee Basin (green) in central Queensland, and the subsurface position of the Galilee Basin displayed conceptually. Note: The conceptual section displays basins along line A−A’ from 0 km to ~4.5 km subsurface.

The Galilee Basin occupies a total area of approximately 249,000 km². The basin is exposed at the surface in the east and north-east. In all other areas the basin lies beneath the Eromanga, Lake Eyre and other smaller Cenozoic basins. The subsurface geology of the Galilee Basin and its overlying basins is understood from 33,213 line km of 2D seismic data and 3,097 boreholes within the geological extent of the basin (Figure 2). Approximately 220 boreholes intersect the Galilee Basin. Borehole and seismic data help to define basin architecture. The Galilee Basin has a maximum modelled thickness of ~2,800 m. Up to ~2,300 m of sedimentary rocks of the Eromanga and Lake Eyre basins overlie the Galilee Basin. Table 1 summarises key structural and geological information from the Galilee Basin region, including geological age, tectonic setting and structures.

Figure 2. Distribution of 2D seismic survey lines and borehole locations in the Galilee Basin region and surrounds. Figure 2 data: Derived from All borehole and well locations – Queensland (Queensland Government, 2022a); Seismic survey 2D – Queensland (Queensland Government, 2022b). The Galilee Basin extents are from the Australian Geological Provinces Database (Raymond et al., 2018). Background image is the GEODATA 9 second digital elevation model, version 3 (hillshade) (Hutchinson et al., 2008).

Table 1. Summary of key structural and geological information from the Galilee Basin. Age: Late Mississippi (Serpukhovian) (~326 Ma) to Late Triassic (Carnian) (~235 Ma); Area: 249,000 km² of central Queensland; Maximum thickness: 2,800 m; Maximum depth to base (m AHD): 2,800 m; Tectonic setting: No consensus. Backarc/mechanical extension, thermal subsidence, contractional (foreland loading/dynamic platform tilting) phases. Considered intracratonic by others; Key structures: Lovelle Depression, Koburra Trough, Springsure Shelf, Pleasant Creek Arch, Powell Depression, Barcaldine Ridge, Canaway Fault, Hopkins Thrust System; Basin overlies: Adavale Basin, Drummond Basin, Belyando Basin, Thomson Orogeny; Basin underlies: Eromanga Basin, Lake Eyre Basin, Noranside Basin, Springvale Basin, Old Cork Basin; Basins adjacent: Cooper Basin, Bowen Basin.
Notes: m AHD = metres with respect to the Australian Height Datum.

Structural elements: Crustal movements shape geological basins during and after sediment deposition. Structural elements are the basic geological features produced by crustal deformation, such as basement, faults and folds (i.e. synclines and anticlines). Structural elements maps capture the key geological features created by deformation events. Structural offsets affect regional groundwater flow and are key to locating areas of resource potential. The geologic basement is the surface beneath which sedimentary rocks are not found. Stratigraphic frameworks: The arrangement and description of rock layers (strata) in an area are captured in a stratigraphic framework. Strata may be organised into units based primarily on rock character (lithostratigraphy), geological age (biostratigraphy and chronostratigraphy), or rocks of the same geological age bound by surfaces of erosion and deposition (sequence stratigraphy). The frameworks included in this package display lithostratigraphic and, where available, other stratigraphic arrangements for the Galilee and overlying basins.

Core photography: Rock may be collected during borehole drilling as a cylindrical core sample. Core is used to measure rock properties, such as lithology, grain size and porosity. These properties are important for evaluating groundwater systems and hydrocarbon resource potential. Core sampling is also used to support stratigraphic and gross depositional environment interpretations. Core images are provided in this data package as a cross-reference to the interpretations that underlie the groundwater and resource assessments of key intervals.

Several structural elements are mapped in the subsurface Galilee Basin region, mainly in the west and south (Figure 3). The 3 locations of maximum sediment thickness, or depocentres, in the Galilee Basin are the Lovelle Depression in the north-west, the Koburra Trough in the north-east and Powell Depression in the south. Key structures (folds, faults or basement structures) controlling basin architecture include the Springsure Shelf, Canaway Fault and Pleasant Creek Arch. The Springsure Shelf is a basement high that marks the eastern region of the basin and connects it with the Bowen Basin. The Canaway Fault coincides with a ridge that marks the south-western boundary with the Cooper Basin. The Pleasant Creek Arch is a structural high of the underlying Adavale Basin that influenced sediment deposition in the Galilee Basin. Some of the structural elements shown in Figure 3 are expressed in the overlying Eromanga Basin. Structural elements may influence aquifer connectivity and are relevant for the groundwater conceptual model of the Galilee Basin region (Hostetler et al., 2023). They also influence areas where conventional hydrocarbon resources maybe trapped.

Figure 3. Galilee Basin region structural elements imposed on a surface map showing depth to the base of the Galilee Basin. Note: Depth is m AHD. Figure 3 data: The structural elements are combined for the Galilee, Eromanga and Lake Eyre basins. Depth to base of the Galilee basin and faults are taken from the Bioregional Assessment Program (2014, 2015). Structural elements and related structures are taken from the Onshore Basin Inventory (Carr et al., 2016) and l’Anson et al. (2018).

Stratigraphic charts are included in this data package for each of the sedimentary basins indicated in Figure 4 for the Galilee Basin region. The charts display groups and formations and their dominant lithology, plotted against geological time. These are arranged into play intervals and hydrostratigraphic intervals to the level that current knowledge allows. Play intervals and hydrostratigraphic intervals are used by the Trusted Environmental and Geological Information (TEGI) Program for resource and groundwater assessments. Where relevant, other related stratigraphic information is included, along with information on potential petroleum, geological storage of carbon, and groundwater systems. Play intervals are defined as a set of rocks formed by the same geologic circumstances, bounded by major geological events. These events may be prolonged periods of non-deposition or erosion (hiatuses) or tectonic events. For this reason, the charts include depositional environments, basin phases and tectonic events with time.

Hydrostratigraphic intervals are grouped geological units that have a similar character influencing the distribution and movement of groundwater, including aquifers. Petroleum systems describe the geological elements necessary to generate and store hydrocarbons. Source rock, reservoir and seal intervals are relevant for conventional hydrocarbon exploration. Strata that are targets for unconventional hydrocarbon exploration are also indicated. Geological storage of carbon (GSC) describes the geological elements required for the injection and containment of carbon dioxide underground. Intervals with GSC potential are shown.

Figure 5. Example core image from the Galilee Basin Betts Creek − Rewan Play interval. Figure 5 data: Core photography of GSQ Hughenden 3-4R obtained by Carmine Wainman. Cores stored at the Exploration Data Centre, Brisbane, Queensland. See appendices for core photographs from other play intervals. We acknowledge the staff at the Queensland and Geoscience Australia core libraries for their assistance with sampling.

Figure 4. Simplified stratigraphic chart of sedimentary basins in the Galilee Basin region and underlying pre-Devonian rocks. Note: Red lines denote hiatuses. Figure 4 data: Gradstein et al. (2020). See metadata statements and appendices for source information.

Representative images of core samples are used to illustrate the dominant rock types and other geological features of stratigraphic intervals. Observations are used to make interpretations of gross depositional environments and help to guide resource and groundwater assessments. Figure 5 is an example from the Betts Creek-Rewan Play interval (124.24–128.24 and 90.20–90.30 metres below ground level from the GSQ Hughenden 3-4R core. The core hosts sandstone, claystone and coal lithologies and are interpreted to represent fluvial and mire environments.

Geological data within this package is based mostly on publicly available borehole data. Confidence in these data is calculated and mapped using the following parameters: the date each borehole was acquired; the total depth the borehole was drilled to; and the spatial separation between boreholes. Data confidence in the Galilee Basin region subsurface geology presented in this package remains low due to the low density of borehole and the depth to which the boreholes were drilled to. Data confidence is higher in several places where there is coal seam gas production, including in the Aramac Trough (Figure 6). Approximately 13% of boreholes exceed depths of greater than 1,000 m below ground level. See Wainman et al. (2023) for 2D seismic confidence.

The low density of borehole data combined with shallow drilling depths limits meaningful interpretations of sedimentary architectures and confident regional interpretations of gross depositional environments across the Galilee Basin region. To address data and knowledge gaps, complementary activities could include well log conditioning and refinement of stratigraphic frameworks with new robust age data; and activities such as drilling a stratigraphic borehole that intersects the deeper play intervals (e.g. Jericho Play interval) to improve understanding of the Galilee Basin regional geology.
