passages.t: Publicly available geology data are compiled to provide a common information base for resource development and regulatory decisions in the north Bowen Basin region (Figure 1). This data guide gives examples of how the compiled data can be used. It supports a data package that presents core photographs, existing knowledge of the stratigraphy, and structural elements for the north Bowen Basin and the overlying Cenozoic basins. Stratigraphic frameworks capture the geological groups and formations that make up the sedimentary sequence in the north Bowen Basin region. The north Bowen Basin has 5 stratigraphic groups. From deepest to shallowest, these are the Lizzie Creek Group, Back Creek Group, Blackwater Group, Rewan Group and Clematis Group. Overlying the north Bowen Basin are the geological formations of Cenozoic basins. The north Bowen Basin has 5 play intervals, which are consolidated into one hydrostratigraphic interval. Overlying the north Bowen Basin are 1 Cenozoic play interval and 1 hydrostratigraphic interval. The geological groups and formations in the play intervals and hydrostratigraphic intervals are summarised in the stratigraphic charts included with this data package. Structural elements maps summarise where the sedimentary sequence has been deposited and later deformed by crustal movements. Structure information is used in assessing the geological potential for resources and interpreting groundwater flow and connectivity at the basin scale.

The stratigraphic frameworks and structural elements provide the basic geological context for the north Bowen Basin region geological, resource and environmental assessments. Keywords: north Bowen Basin, structure, seismic, boreholes, stratigraphy, core, play intervals, hydrostratigraphic intervals, confidence.

Figure 1. Geographic location of the north Bowen Basin (blue) in central Queensland and the subsurface position of the north Bowen Basin displayed conceptually. Note: The conceptual section displays basins along line A−A’ from 0 km to ~4.5 km subsurface.

The north Bowen Basin occupies a total area of approximately 83,100 km². In the north, the basin is exposed at the surface. In all other areas, the basin lies beneath eastern extensional basins of Cenozoic age, including the Duaringa and Emerald basins. The subsurface geology of the north Bowen Basin and its overlying basins is understood from 12,360 line km of 2D seismic data and 9,435 boreholes within the geological extent of the basin (Figure 2). Approximately 9% of boreholes reach total depths greater than 1,000 m below ground level. Borehole and seismic data help to define basin architecture. The north Bowen Basin has a maximum modelled thickness of ~10,325 m. Up to ~1,200 m of Cenozoic sedimentary rocks (Australian Stratigraphic Units Database, 2022) overlie the north Bowen Basin. Table 1 summarises key structural and geological information from the north Bowen Basin region, including age, tectonic setting and structures.

Figure 2. Distribution of 2D seismic survey lines and borehole locations in the north Bowen Basin region and surrounds. Figure 2 data: Derived from All borehole and well locations – Queensland (Queensland Government, 2022a); Seismic survey 2D – Queensland (Queensland Government, 2022b). The north Bowen Basin extents are from the Australian Geological Provinces Database (Raymond et al., 2018). Background image is the GEODATA 9 second digital elevation model, version 3 (hillshade) (Hutchinson et al., 2008).

Table 1. Summary of key structural and geological information for the north Bowen Basin. Age: Cisuralian (Asselian) (~299 Ma) to Middle Triassic (Ladinian) (~238 Ma); Area: 83,114 km² of south-west Queensland; Maximum thickness: >10,000 m; Maximum depth to base (m AHD): 0 to >10,000 m; Tectonic setting: Extension (Cisuralian), thermal subsidence (Guadalupian) and foreland (Lopingian to Middle Triassic) phases; Key structures: Taroom Trough, Denison Trough, Springsure Shelf, Comet Ridge, Collinsville Shelf, Capella Block, Nebo Synclinorium; Basin overlies: Thomson Orogen, Drummond Basin, Anakie Province; Basin underlies: Duaringa Basin, Emerald Basin, Biloela Basin, Redbank Basin, Yaamba Basin, Woorabinda Basin, Exevale Formation; Basins adjacent: Galilee Basin, Gunnedah Basin.
Notes: m AHD = metres with respect to the Australian Height Datum.

Structural elements: Crustal movements shape geological basins during and after sediment deposition. Structural elements are the basic geological features produced by crustal deformation, such as basement, faults and folds (i.e. synclines and anticlines). Structural elements maps capture the key geological features created by deformation events. Structural offsets affect regional groundwater flow and are key to locating areas of resource potential. The geologic basement is the surface beneath which sedimentary rocks are not found. Stratigraphic frameworks: The arrangement and description of rock layers (strata) in an area are captured in a stratigraphic framework. Strata may be organised into units based primarily on rock character (lithostratigraphy), geological age (biostratigraphy and chronostratigraphy), or rocks of the same geological age bound by surfaces of erosion and deposition (sequence stratigraphy). The frameworks included in this package display lithostratigraphic and, where available, other stratigraphic arrangements for the Adavale and overlying basins.

Core photography: Rock may be collected during borehole drilling as a cylindrical core sample. Core is used to measure rock properties, such as lithology, grain size and porosity. These properties are important for evaluating groundwater systems and hydrocarbon resource potential. Core is also used to support stratigraphic and gross depositional environment interpretations. Core images are provided in this data package as a cross-reference to the interpretations that underlie the groundwater and resource assessments of key intervals.

Several structural elements are mapped in the subsurface north Bowen Basin region, mainly in the west and south (Figure 3). No open source surfaces were available for download from the north Bowen Basin for basin modelling. The 2 locations of maximum sediment thickness, or depocentres, in the north Bowen Basin are the Taroom Trough in the southern north Bowen Basin and the Denison Trough in the south-west north Bowen Basin. Key structures (folds, faults and basement structures) controlling basin architecture include the Comet Ridge, the Nebo Synclinorium and the Capella Block. The Springsure Shelf is a basement high in the western region of the basin and connects it with the Galilee Basin. The Comet Ridge is one of the main tectonic units in the basin and was a positive feature during deposition separating the Taroom Trough from the Denison Trough. Some of the structural elements shown in Figure 3 are expressed in the overlying Cenozoic basins. Structural elements may influence aquifer connectivity (Hostetler et al., 2023). They also influence areas where conventional hydrocarbon resources may be trapped.

Figure 3. North Bowen Basin region structural elements imposed on a surface map showing depth to the base of the north Bowen Basin. Note: Depth is m AHD. Figure 3 data: The structural elements are combined for the north Bowen and overlying Cenozoic basins. Depth to basement is derived from OZ SEEBASE® 2021, Geognostics (2021). Structures (including faults) are derived from the Queensland Geology and Structural Framework (2012) and the Bowen and Surat Regional Structural Framework (2008). Structural elements are taken from Draper (2013).

Stratigraphic charts are included in this data package for each of the sedimentary basins indicated in Figure 4 for the north Bowen Basin region. The charts display groups and formations and their dominant lithology, plotted against geological time. These are arranged into play intervals and hydrostratigraphic intervals to the level that current knowledge allows. Play intervals and hydrostratigraphic intervals are used by the Trusted Environmental and Geological Information (TEGI) Program for resource and groundwater assessments. Where relevant, other related stratigraphic information is included, along with information on potential petroleum, geological storage of carbon, and groundwater systems. Play intervals are defined as a set of rocks formed by the same geologic circumstances, bounded by major geological events. These events may be prolonged periods of non-deposition or erosion (hiatuses) or tectonic events. For this reason, the charts include depositional environments, basin phases and tectonic events with time.

Hydrostratigraphic intervals are grouped geological units that have a similar character influencing the distribution and movement of groundwater, including aquifers. Petroleum systems describe the geological elements necessary to generate and store hydrocarbons. Source rock, reservoir and seal intervals are relevant for conventional hydrocarbon exploration. Strata that are targets for unconventional hydrocarbon exploration are also indicated. Geological storage of carbon (GSC) describes the geological elements required for the injection and containment of carbon dioxide underground. Intervals with GSC potential are shown.

Figure 4. Simplified stratigraphic chart of sedimentary basins of the north Bowen Basin region and underlying pre-Carboniferous rocks. Note: Red lines denote hiatuses. Figure 4 data: Gradstein et al. (2020). See metadata statements and appendices for source information.

Representative images of core samples are used to illustrate the dominant rock types and other geological features of stratigraphic intervals. Observations are used to make interpretations of gross depositional environments and help to guide resource and groundwater assessments. Figure 5 is an example from the Upper Back Creek Play interval (700.35–703.85 and 697–697.26 metres below ground level from the GSQ Taroom 10 core. The core hosts claystone, siltstone and sandstone and are interpreted to represent a deltaic environment.

Figure 5 data: Core photography of GSQ Taroom 10 obtained by Carmine Wainman. Cores stored at the Exploration Data Centre, Brisbane, Queensland. See appendices for core photographs from other play intervals. We acknowledge the staff at the Queensland and Geoscience Australia core libraries for their assistance with sampling.

A play interval, for the purpose of resource assessments, consists of an interval of sedimentary rocks formed by the same geological processes. Play intervals capture regionally significant reservoirs for potential hydrocarbon accumulations or the geological storage of carbon (GSC). Groundwater systems are further grouped into hydrostratigraphic intervals that capture key aquifers and aquitards. Play interval boundaries correspond to major geological events that interrupt or change basin sedimentation, such as tectonic events. Gross depositional environment maps, such as the example given in Figure 6, are maps of the interpreted environments where sediment in a play was deposited, such as on a coastal plain. The interpretations are based on the characteristics of rocks and their associated geophysical attributes retrieved during borehole drilling. Play intervals (Table 2) can include both reservoir and seal rocks, which can correspond to aquifers and aquitards in regional groundwater systems. The hydrostratigraphic intervals for groundwater characterisation correspond either directly to play intervals or to sets of plays where aquifers are connected or not well defined.
Figure 6. Upper Back Creek Play interval gross depositional environment map. Figure 6 data: Gross depositional map from Furnass et al. (2023). Maps derived from Fielding et al. (2001).

Table 2. Summary of north Bowen Basin region play interval properties. Cenozoic play interval: hydrostratigraphic interval Cenozoic hydrogeological unit; approximate thickness 1,200 m; depositional environments: Fluvial to lacustrine, intraplate volcanism. Clematis play interval: hydrostratigraphic interval Clematis aquifer; approximate thickness 4,870 m; depositional environments: Fluvial to fluviolacustrine. Blackwater–Rewan play interval: hydrostratigraphic interval –; approximate thickness 1,650 m; depositional environments: Fluvial (north) to offshore marine (south). Upper Back Creek play interval: hydrostratigraphic interval –; approximate thickness 2,930 m; depositional environments: Coastal deltaic to offshore marine. Collinsville play interval: hydrostratigraphic interval –; approximate thickness 250 m; depositional environments: Deltaic (north) to marine shelf (south). Reids Dome play interval: hydrostratigraphic interval –; approximate thickness 3,000 m; depositional environments: Back arc to north, fluviolacustrine to south.

Geological information within this data package is mostly based on open-source borehole data (Figure 7) and 2D seismic lines (Figure 8). Confidence in 2D seismic data is calculated and mapped using the following parameters: the date each seismic line was acquired; the line km of 2D seismic shot; and the spatial separation of 2D seismic lines from each other. Confidence in borehole data is calculated and mapped using the following parameters: the date each borehole was acquired; the total depth the borehole was drilled to; and the spatial separation between boreholes. Data confidence in the north Bowen Basin region subsurface geology presented in this package is varied. For borehole data, confidence is low due to few boreholes reaching more than 1,000 m below ground level or to the base of the north Bowen Basin – e.g. in the vicinity of the Nebo Synclinorium and on the Collinsville Shelf (Figure 7). For 2D seismic data, confidence is variable across the basin: it is medium to high in the vicinity of the Folded Zone, where short, closely spaced lines have been acquired; in contrast, confidence is low to medium in the Nebo Synclinorium and Denison Trough, where fewer 2D lines have been acquired (Figure 8). In combination, there is insufficient data to constrain regional basin architecture and determine stratigraphic relationships.

Figure 7. Geological data confidence map for the north Bowen Basin region, based on the drill date, total depth and spatial separation of boreholes. Figures 7 and 8 data: Derived from All boreholes and wells – Queensland (Queensland Government, 2022a) and Seismic survey 2D – Queensland (Queensland Government, 2022b).

To address data and knowledge gaps, complementary activities could include well log conditioning and refinement of stratigraphic frameworks with new robust age data; and activities such as drilling a stratigraphic borehole that intersects the deeper play intervals (e.g. Reids Dome Play interval) and acquisition of deep regional 2D seismic lines in regions with limited and uneven data coverage in order to improve understanding of the north Bowen Basin regional geology.
